title: The People You Choose Can Make or Break Your Life | Lessons from Stanford
summary: Part two of Cherie's masterclass on the late Stanford GSB professor Joel Peterson's 'Engineering a Remarkable Life' course, covering the pillars 'someone to love' and 'work to do.' The sisters walk through Peterson's own complementary marriage, an exercise for operationalizing relationships with objectives and measures, a must-have vs nice-to-have partner list, his definition of a great career, and how to survive the inevitable bad decade.

ideas.idea: A remarkable life rests on three pillars: a person to be, someone to love, and work to do.
ideas.detail: Part one covered inward reflection on family history and values; part two covers constructing relationships and career. Jean notes HBS never taught anything like this as curriculum, while Stanford gave two credits for it.

ideas.idea: The most consistent finding of Harvard's 85-year happiness study is that positive relationships, not career, money, exercise or diet, keep us happier and healthier and help us live longer.
ideas.detail: Peterson's slides cite the study begun in 1938 with 724 participants questioned at two-year intervals. The hosts say this is why the podcast covers money, power and love, including platonic, family and self love.

ideas.idea: The person you choose as your partner is the most important decision you will make, because it shapes how you feel every single day.
ideas.detail: Whether you come home stressed or relaxed depends on your person. Peterson brought his wife Diana into class so students could hear how the life was engineered from her side; being 'self-partnered' as Emma Watson put it is equally legitimate if nobody meets your criteria.

ideas.idea: Look for a partner who is complementary rather than identical, like a striver paired with roots.
ideas.detail: Peterson describes himself as the striver climbing Kilimanjaro and planning trips while Diana is the tree keeping the family rooted in home and traditions; with their seven kids he came from above with discipline while she got down on the floor at their level. Cherie likens it to a founder hiring for the skills they lack.

ideas.idea: Couples should take stock of both family histories and intentionally choose which customs to carry into the next generation and which generational traumas to break.
ideas.detail: Building on the family-history exercise from part one, Peterson taught that it is up to both partners to pick the best of both backgrounds; Cherie had never thought about it that deliberately before.

ideas.idea: Operationalize love: list five to seven key people, set an objective for each relationship and define how you will measure it, because flowy love without objectives falls by the wayside.
ideas.detail: Cherie's example for best friend Esha: objective 'reignite our friendship,' measures monthly calls, a yearly ski trip, small touchpoints like sending memes, and monthly handwritten cards. Other objectives include 'maintain homeostasis,' 'deepen relationship,' 'grow deeper in love'; measures include weekly FaceTimes, weekly dates and planned trips.

ideas.idea: Listing your five to seven people is also an accounting exercise that reveals whether your energy matches your intentions.
ideas.detail: Jean points out you may discover you spend lots of energy on someone you don't intend to be close with, or only talk monthly to someone you want to build with; Cherie crossed an ex-best-friend off her list, freeing time for the others.

ideas.idea: Co-founders who are also sisters, co-hosts and roommates need an explicit objective for their relationship: staying fulfilling, energy-giving and fun, not just mission-driven.
ideas.detail: Doing the exercise live for each other, the sisters set the baseline as not pissing each other off and joke that the measure is co-founder therapy.

ideas.idea: Write two lists for a life partner, must-haves and nice-to-haves, and be honest that some attributes like physical attractiveness fade over 20-30 years.
ideas.detail: Peterson's attribute list includes shared values, strong work ethic, parallel politics, family compatibility, common roots, sense of humor, a great gene pool ('hybrid vigor'), devotion and fidelity, similar tastes, smart and shared vocations. Jean says parallel politics never came up for her until the last couple of years but now clearly belongs on the list.

ideas.idea: Building a great career means helping others become a respected member of a winning team doing something meaningful, and if any one element is missing it doesn't work.
ideas.detail: Peterson, who led organizations of hundreds of thousands, frames work as purpose, not just money or progression. The hosts note everyone wants to be respected and valued, and a good manager's responsibility is to build up the people on their team rather than serve themselves.

ideas.idea: Every long career has incredible highs and lows, and you may have an entire bad decade; prepare to survive it and don't let it ruin you.
ideas.detail: Peterson was sued by his former company in litigation that dragged on for around ten years, which he called 'a really bad decade'; out of it he founded Peterson Partners, now Peterson Ventures. Cherie at 27 was shaken that a bad decade was even possible, which showed her how long life is.

ideas.idea: Do everything possible to avoid being in a lawsuit, because litigation consumes your mindshare for years.
ideas.detail: Peterson's side lesson from his own suit: if there are threats of a lawsuit, resolve it before it becomes one; it is miserable and always in the back of your mind.

ideas.idea: Rain will fall on your fields, whether at work, in health or through a death in the family, so fortify yourself and your partnership before it happens.
ideas.detail: The partner you choose is the anchor who gets you through the hardest times, tying the 'someone to love' and 'work to do' pillars together; the thriving gets posted on LinkedIn but surviving is the part nobody talks about.

ideas.idea: Memorizing iconic texts builds inner strength for hard times, a practice Peterson follows himself and required of his children.
ideas.detail: He cites prisoners of war who stayed sane by reciting memorized material; he knows the Gettysburg Address, Bible verses and French passages by heart. The sisters recall memorizing Chinese poems as kids and note the tradition spans cultures.
